title: SBAR Communication Framework
summary: Using the SBAR framework for structured, concise clinical communication with providers and team members.
steps: Prepare BEFORE calling: have the patient's chart in front of you. Know: current vitals, admission diagnosis, relevant history, current medications, labs/imaging results.
S — SITUATION: Who you are, where you are, what is happening right now.
'This is Nurse [Name] calling from [Unit]. I'm calling about [Patient Name], Room [#]. The reason I'm calling is [specific concern].'
B — BACKGROUND: relevant clinical context.
'Patient is a [age]-year-old [sex] admitted for [diagnosis]. Relevant history includes [PMHx]. Current medications include [key meds].'
A — ASSESSMENT: your clinical conclusion.
'I think the problem is... OR I'm not sure what the problem is, but I am concerned because...'
R — RECOMMENDATION: what you are asking for.
'I would like you to [come evaluate the patient / order a medication / clarify the treatment plan / etc.].'
Document the call: time, provider name, SBAR content, orders received, read-back completed.
Read back ALL verbal orders to confirm accuracy.
If concerned response was inadequate: escalate up the chain of command.
safetyTips: Incomplete handoff communication is the #1 cause of adverse events in hospitals.
Always read back verbal orders — it is a Joint Commission requirement and prevents medication errors.
If you are dismissed but remain concerned — escalate. Document that you escalated.

title: Structured Nurse-to-Nurse Handoff Report (I-PASS / SBAR)
summary: Providing a complete and accurate patient handoff to the oncoming nurse at shift change.
equipment: Current EMAR, MAR, and chart access
steps: Use a standardized format. I-PASS:
I — Illness severity: stable, watcher, unstable.
P — Patient summary: one-line summary of who the patient is, admission reason, course.
A — Action list: pending tasks, labs to follow, calls to make.
S — Situation awareness: what could go wrong? What should the next nurse watch for?
S — Synthesis: oncoming nurse reads back/summarizes plan.
Cover the following for each patient:
- Name, age, diagnosis, day of admission.
- Code status, allergies.
- Lines/tubes/drains and last assessment of each.
- IV access type and location.
- Last vitals, pain score, neurological status.
- PRN medications given last shift.
- Pending labs, cultures, imaging.
- Specific concerns for the upcoming shift.
Perform bedside handoff when possible — patient can contribute and nurse can visually verify.
Do NOT hand off tasks that can be completed before leaving your shift.
safetyTips: Incomplete handoffs are the #1 communication failure in adverse event reviews.
Bedside handoff reduces errors and increases patient satisfaction — make it standard.
Never hand off an unstable patient without ensuring the oncoming nurse acknowledges the situation.
keyTakeaways: I-PASS: Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness, Synthesis
Don't hand off tasks you can complete

title: Critical Lab Value Recognition & Reporting
summary: Recognizing critical lab values and reporting them to the provider using a structured closed-loop communication process.
steps: KNOW your facility's critical lab value list (examples):
K+ <2.5 or >6.5 mEq/L
Na+ <120 or >160 mEq/L
Glucose <40 or >500 mg/dL
Hgb <7 g/dL
Platelets <20,000
INR >5.0
Troponin positive (any)
Lactate >4 mmol/L
ASSESS the patient clinically — is the result consistent with how the patient looks?
CALL the provider IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait until rounds.
Use SBAR: state the critical value, patient's clinical status, and what action you are recommending or need.
READ BACK any verbal orders received.
Document: value, time reported, provider name, orders received, and patient's clinical response.
Follow up to confirm orders were acted on.
safetyTips: Critical values require immediate action — a delayed call for a K+ of 6.8 can mean a fatal arrhythmia.
Document the time the result was reported. Medicolegally, undocumented notification = no notification.
If the provider is unresponsive, escalate up the chain of command — and document this.
documentation: Orders received and time of documentation
keyTakeaways: Immediate notification — never wait until rounds

title: Medication Reconciliation
summary: Comparing a patient's medication orders to all medications they have been taking to avoid discrepancies.
steps: Obtain the BEST possible medication history (BPMH) on admission:
Ask patient AND family/caregiver.
Review pharmacy records, PCP medication list, discharge summaries.
Ask specifically about: OTC medications, vitamins, supplements, herbal products, topical medications, PRN medications.
Ask about allergies and the specific reaction type (anaphylaxis vs. GI intolerance).
Compare home medications to admission orders: identify intentional changes, omissions, dosing discrepancies.
Flag HIGH-RISK medications for mandatory reconciliation: anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, cardiac medications.
Reconcile at TRANSITIONS: admission, transfer between units, discharge.
DISCHARGE: compare final hospital medication list to home medications. Explicitly communicate what is new, what is changed, what is stopped.
Provide patient with a complete, up-to-date medication list in plain language on discharge.
safetyTips: Medication reconciliation errors at discharge are a leading cause of hospital readmissions and adverse events.
Anticoagulants are the #1 drug class involved in reconciliation errors. Document dose, route, indication, and monitoring requirements.
Unintentional omission of home medications (e.g., beta-blockers, seizure meds) is as dangerous as a wrong medication.
documentation: Discharge medication list given to patient
keyTakeaways: Patient gets a written updated list at discharge
